punctuated:
吳國倫〔貫湖廣武昌府興國州軍籍，州學生，治《易經》，字明可，行五，年二十七，正月二十一日生〕。曾祖澄，祖義，父顏，母李氏。永感下，兄國佐、國位、國典、國化，娶陳氏。湖廣鄉試第一名，會試第三百十六名。

王杰〔貫浙江湖州府烏程縣匠籍，國子生，治《春秋》，字子秀，行二，年三十六，九月十三日生〕。曾祖鏞，祖盤，父滔〔醫學正術〕，母朱氏，繼母閔氏。永感下，兄材，弟榜〔監生〕、本〔監生〕、杏、梯、樂、桐，娶張氏。應天府鄉試第八十二名，會試第七十九名。

鄭伯興〔貫直隸常州府無錫縣民籍，國子生，治《詩經》，字子振，行三，年三十四，五月十七日生〕。曾祖恪，祖尊，父鉞，母傅氏。具慶下，兄伯強、伯達，娶顧氏。應天府鄉試第十三名，會試第二十五名。

康世耀〔貫直隸保定府完縣軍籍，大寧都司保定中衛，縣學增廣生，治《詩經》，字子潜，行一，年二十四，二月二十一日生〕。曾祖有能，祖旺，父馴，母冀氏。重慶下，弟世輝、世烺、世光，娶石氏。順天府鄉試第一百十四名，會試第二百八十一名。
translation_en:
Wu Guolun, of a military household registered in Xingguo Subprefecture, Wuchang Prefecture, Huguang, was a student of the subprefectural school specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Mingke; he ranked fifth among his brothers and was aged twenty-seven, born on the twenty-first day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Cheng, his grandfather Yi, and his father Yan; his mother was née Li. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Guozuo, Guowei, Guodian, and Guohua. His wife was née Chen. He placed first in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 316th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Jie, of an artisan household registered in Wucheng County, Huzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Zixiu; he ranked second among his brothers and was aged thirty-six, born on the thirteenth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yong, his grandfather Pan, and his father Tao, a medical officer in the local medical school. His mother was née Zhu and his stepmother née Min. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Cai; his younger brothers were Bang and Ben, both students of the Directorate of Education, and Xing, Ti, Le, and Tong. His wife was née Zhang. He placed eighty-second in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventy-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zheng Boxing, of a civilian household registered in Wuxi County, Changzhou Prefecture, Zhili, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Zizhen; he ranked third among his brothers and was aged thirty-four, born on the seventeenth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ke, his grandfather Zun, and his father Yue; his mother was née Fu. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Boqiang and Boda. His wife was née Gu. He placed thirteenth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and twenty-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Kang Shiyao, of a military household registered in Wan County, Baoding Prefecture, Zhili, affiliated with the Baoding Central Guard under the Daning Regional Military Commission, was an added-quota student of the county school specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Ziqian; he ranked first among his brothers and was aged twenty-four, born on the twenty-first day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Youneng, his grandfather Wang, and his father Xun; his mother was née Ji. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Shihui, Shilang, and Shiguang. His wife was née Shi. He placed 114th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 281st in the Metropolitan Examination.

貫直隸大名府開州長垣縣民籍 國子生

貫陝西鞏昌府隴西縣軍籍 國子生

曾祖進 祖銳〔壽官〕 父世福 母白氏
具慶下 弟心 娶喬氏

punctuated:
王喬年，貫山東萊州府高密縣民籍，縣學生，治詩經，字耆卿，行一，年二十六，四月初四日生。曾祖仁，祖輔〔府教授〕，父邦憲〔訓導〕，前母張氏，母李氏。慈侍下，娶單氏，繼娶管氏。山東鄉試第五十四名，會試第三百十名。

謝莆，貫山西太原府代州旗籍，國子生，治詩經，字符德，行七，年三十六，五月十八日生。曾祖鐸〔推官〕，祖璽〔按察司僉事贈通議大夫工部右侍郎〕，父國表〔監察御史〕，母吳氏〔封太孺人〕。永感下，兄芝〔按察司副使〕、蘭〔通議大夫兵部右侍郎〕、蕕〔監生〕、菊〔廕生〕，弟苹、萃，娶崔氏，繼娶王氏。山西鄉試第三十名，會試第七十七名。

李體，貫直隸大名府開州長垣縣民籍，國子生，治詩經，字仲全，行四，年四十五，十二月十五日生。曾祖榮，祖泰，父塤〔訓導〕，母陳氏。永感下，娶陳氏。順天府鄉試第一百二十四名，會試第一百八十四名。

王一言，貫陝西鞏昌府隴西縣軍匠籍，國子生，治春秋，字子大，行一，年二十六，三月十二日生。曾祖通，祖銳〔壽官〕，父世福，母巨氏。具慶下，弟心，娶喬氏。陝西鄉試第二十五名，會試第三百九名。
translation_en:
Wang Qiaonian was registered in a civilian household in Gaomi County, Laizhou Prefecture, Shandong, and was a county school student. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Qiqing; he ranked first among his brothers, was twenty-six years old, and was born on the fourth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ren; his grandfather, Fu, was a prefectural school instructor; and his father, Bangxian, was an assistant instructor. His father’s former wife was née Zhang, and his mother was née Li. His mother alone survived. He married a woman née Shan and subsequently a woman née Guan. He placed fifty-fourth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 310th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xie Pu was registered in a banner household [?] in Daizhou, Taiyuan Prefecture, Shanxi, and was a National University student. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Fude; he ranked seventh among his brothers, was thirty-six years old, and was born on the eighteenth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather, Duo, was a prefectural judge. His grandfather, Xi, was an assistant surveillance commissioner, posthumously granted the titles Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Right Vice Minister of Works. His father, Guobiao, was an investigating censor, and his mother, née Wu, was ennobled as Dowager Lady. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Zhi, a surveillance vice commissioner; Lan, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Right Vice Minister of War; You, a National University student; and Ju, a student admitted through hereditary privilege. His younger brothers were Ping and Cui. He married a woman née Cui and subsequently a woman née Wang. He placed thirtieth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and seventy-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Ti was registered in a civilian household in Changyuan County, Kaizhou, Daming Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was a National University student. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Zhongquan; he ranked fourth among his brothers, was forty-five years old, and was born on the fifteenth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Rong; his grandfather was Tai; his father, Xun, was an assistant instructor; and his mother was née Chen. Both parents were deceased. He married a woman née Chen. He placed 124th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 184th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Yiyan was registered in a military artisan household in Longxi County, Gongchang Prefecture, Shaanxi, and was a National University student. He specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Zida; he ranked first among his brothers, was twenty-six years old, and was born on the twelfth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Tong; his grandfather, Rui, held an honorary official title conferred for longevity; his father was Shifu; and his mother was née Ju. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Xin. He married a woman née Qiao. He placed twenty-fifth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 309th in the Metropolitan Examination.

楊乾亨〔貫江西南昌府南昌縣，民籍，國子生，治《詩經》，字啓元，行四，年三十五，十二月十八日生〕。曾祖祐〔都司經歷，進階奉訓大夫〕，祖英〔知縣〕，父元龍，母辜氏。慈侍下，兄益亨、永亨、朗〔國子生〕、明亨、大亨、旦亨，弟信亨、宣亨、謙亨、端亨、光亨、濬亨，娶張氏。江西鄉試第二名，會試第二百五十七名。

張昇〔貫山西澤州陽城縣，民籍，國子生，治《易經》，字伯東，行一，年三十七，正月十一日生〕。曾祖演，祖表，父曉，母王氏。慈侍下，弟冕、鼎，娶尹氏，繼娶王氏。山西鄉試第二十二名，會試第一百十一名。

喬光大〔貫山西太原府忻州定襄縣，軍籍，國子生，治《書經》，字子充，行一，年三十八，八月初十日生〕。曾祖瑛〔壽官〕，祖震〔知州〕，父茂亨〔州吏目〕，母郭氏。慈侍下，弟光遠、光宙、光宣、光裕、光祚、光武，娶楊氏。山西鄉試第十八名，會試第一百九名。
translation_en:
Xia Shi, registered in Fengcheng County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to an artisan household and was a county school student. He specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Tingzhan, and he ranked sixth in his family. He was twenty-five, born on the twenty-ninth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Rishui [?]; his grandfather, Zongjie; and his father, Ruoshui, an annual tribute student. His mother was née Zhou, and his stepmother née Sun. Both parents were living. His wife was née Xiong. He placed thirty-eighth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and fifty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Qianheng, registered in Nanchang County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was an Imperial University student. He specialized in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Qiyuan, and he ranked fourth in his family. He was thirty-five, born on the eighteenth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was You, Registrar in a Regional Military Commission, advanced in honorary rank to Grand Master for Instruction; his grandfather was Ying, a County Magistrate; and his father was Yuanlong. His mother was née Gu. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His elder brothers were Yiheng, Yongheng, Lang (an Imperial University student), Mingheng, Daheng, and Danheng; his younger brothers were Xinheng, Xuanheng, Qianheng 謙亨, Duanheng, Guangheng, and Junheng. His wife was née Zhang. He placed second in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 257th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Sheng, registered in Yangcheng County, Zezhou, Shanxi, belonged to a civilian household and was an Imperial University student. He specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Bodong, and he ranked first in his family. He was thirty-seven, born on the eleventh day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yan; his grandfather, Biao; and his father, Xiao. His mother was née Wang. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His younger brothers were Mian and Ding. His wife was née Yin; he subsequently married a woman née Wang. He placed twenty-second in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 111th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Qiao Guangda, registered in Dingxiang County, Xinzhou, Taiyuan Prefecture, Shanxi, belonged to a military household and was an Imperial University student. He specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Zichong, and he ranked first in his family. He was thirty-eight, born on the tenth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ying, an honorary official recognized for longevity; his grandfather was Zhen, a Department Magistrate; and his father was Maoheng, a Department Clerk. His mother was née Guo. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His younger brothers were Guangyuan, Guangzhou, Guangxuan, Guangyu, Guangzuo, and Guangwu. His wife was née Yang. He placed eighteenth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 109th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Xu Yue, courtesy name Wensheng, was registered in a civilian household in Jiaxing County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Documents, he was fourth in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the twenty-sixth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Gang; his grandfather, Jie; his father, Wu, an Assistant Instructor; and his mother, née Zhu. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Zhuo, Yao, and He. He married a woman née Ge. He ranked eightieth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 124th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ding Xikong, courtesy name Yanxue, was registered in a civilian household in Zhaoyuan County, Dengzhou Prefecture, Shandong. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty, and born on the twenty-second day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Zhong; his grandfather, Xiang; his father, Hao, a Sacrificial Official; and his mother, née Liu. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Xiyin. He married a woman née Liu and subsequently a woman née Sun. He ranked sixtieth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and fifty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wen Jie, courtesy name Kesheng, was registered in a civilian household in Nanchong County, Shunqing Prefecture, Sichuan. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-four, and born on the fourth day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Tingju; his grandfather, Ziying, an Instructor; and his father, Zao. His father's former wife was née Wang, his mother was née Liu, and his stepmother was also née Liu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was De, and his younger brothers were Yang and Sheng. He married a woman née Yi. He ranked twenty-second in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 283rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ding Yongcheng, courtesy name Ziguan, was registered in a military household in Dezhou, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged forty-one, and born on the sixteenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Zhen; his grandfather, Sui; his father, Kui; his mother, née Tang; and his stepmother, née Li. Both parents were living. He married a woman née Zhang and subsequently a woman née Chen. He ranked forty-eighth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and thirty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

王鈇〔貫武驤左衞軍籍，浙江東陽縣人，國子生，治書經，字德威，行四，年三十七，四月十四日生〕。曾祖邦治，祖通，父睿，前母郭氏，母和氏。慈侍下，兄鉞、釗、鐸，弟錐，娶董氏。順天府鄉試第五十二名，會試第二百五十九名。

鍾崇武〔貫江西南昌府南昌縣民籍，國子生，治禮記，字季烈，行二，年三十四，十月二十二日生〕。曾祖叔顯，祖光，父任〔壽官〕，母田氏。具慶下，兄崇文，娶胡氏。江西鄉試第五名，會試第十名。

陳治安〔貫貴州宣慰司軍籍，直隸崑山縣人，宣慰司學增廣生，治詩經，字超誼，行一，年二十九，四月十一日生〕。曾祖晟，祖鋭，父恕，母耿氏。具慶下，娶李氏。貴州鄉試第十八名，會試第二百二十名。

萬虞龍〔貫江西南昌府南昌縣民籍，國子生，治詩經，字言卿，行七，年二十九，五月初六日生〕。曾祖韞華，祖鍾秀〔壽官〕，父開禮〔州判官〕，前母熊氏，母林氏。具慶下，兄虞佐，娶劉氏。江西鄉試第八十二名，會試第十五名。
translation_en:
Wang Fu, registered in a military household of the Wuxiang Left Guard and originally from Dongyang County, Zhejiang, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Dewei; he ranked fourth among his brothers and was aged thirty-seven, born on the fourteenth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Bangzhi, his grandfather Tong, and his father Rui; his father's former wife was née Guo, and his mother was née He. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Yue, Zhao, and Duo, and his younger brother was Zhui. His wife was née Dong. He placed fifty-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 259th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhong Chongwu, registered in a civilian household of Nanchang County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Record of Rites. His courtesy name was Jilie; he ranked second among his brothers and was aged thirty-four, born on the twenty-second day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shuxian, his grandfather Guang, and his father Ren, who held an honorary official title conferred for longevity; his mother was née Tian. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Chongwen, and his wife was née Hu. He placed fifth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and tenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Zhi'an, registered in a military household of the Guizhou Pacification Commission and originally from Kunshan County in the directly administered metropolitan region, was an added-quota student at the Pacification Commission's school, specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Chaoyi; he ranked first among his brothers and was aged twenty-nine, born on the eleventh day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Sheng, his grandfather Rui, and his father Shu; his mother was née Geng. Both parents were living, and his wife was née Li. He placed eighteenth in the Guizhou Provincial Examination and 220th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wan Yulong, registered in a civilian household of Nanchang County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Yanqing; he ranked seventh among his brothers and was aged twenty-nine, born on the sixth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yunhua, his grandfather Zhongxiu, who held an honorary official title conferred for longevity, and his father Kaili, a subprefectural assistant magistrate. His father's former wife was née Xiong, and his mother was née Lin. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Yuzuo, and his wife was née Liu. He placed eighty-second in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and fifteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

孫應魁〔貫直隸松江府上海縣民籍，國子生，治詩經，字元之，行一，年三十二，八月初九日生〕。曾祖寅〔七品散官〕，祖鶚〔刑部司務〕，父繼科〔監生〕，母劉氏。具慶下，弟應詔、應解、應松、應椿、應舉、應兆、應開、應揚，娶唐氏。應天府鄉試第九十八名，會試第一百二十九名。

劉廷舉〔貫湖廣黃州府麻城縣民籍，直隸休寧縣學教諭，治春秋，字直卿，行一，年四十二，正月二十一日生〕。曾祖伯金，祖名山，父濬，前母李氏，母丁氏。永感下，弟廷聘、廷詔、廷棟、廷彦、廷亮、廷碩、廷望、廷對、廷宣，娶李氏。湖廣鄉試第十名，會試第一百三十七名。

錢之選〔貫遼東鐵嶺衛民籍，直隸常熟縣人，衛學生，治詩經，字舜臣，行一，年三十三，七月二十六日生〕。曾祖泰，祖元衿，父表，母王氏。嚴侍下，兄庶〔同科進士〕，弟之逵，娶徐氏，繼娶常氏。順天府鄉試第二十六名，會試第四十二名。

嚴杰〔貫浙江湖州府烏程縣民籍，府學生，治書經，字子俊，行一，年二十九，二月二十三日生〕。曾祖繹〔義官〕，祖釴，父澐〔歳貢生〕，母吳氏。具慶下，弟果、柬，娶蔡氏。浙江鄉試第六名，會試第三十四名。
translation_en:
Sun Yingkui, registered in a civilian household in Shanghai County, Songjiang Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Yuanzhi; he ranked first in birth order and was aged thirty-two, born on the ninth day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Yin, a seventh-rank prestige official; his grandfather was E, an Office Manager in the Ministry of Justice; his father was Jike, a student of the Directorate of Education; and his mother was née Liu. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yingzhao, Yingjie, Yingsong, Yingchun, Yingju, Yingzhao, Yingkai, and Yingyang—the two named Yingzhao being written 應詔 and 應兆 respectively. He married a woman née Tang. He placed ninety-eighth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 129th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Tingju, registered in a civilian household in Macheng County, Huangzhou Prefecture, Huguang, was the Instructor at the county school of Xiuning in the directly administered metropolitan region. He specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Zhiqing; he ranked first in birth order and was aged forty-two, born on the twenty-first day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Bojin, his grandfather was Mingshan, and his father was Jun. His father's former wife was née Li, and his mother was née Ding. Both parents were deceased. His younger brothers were Tingpin, Tingzhao, Tingdong, Tingyan, Tingliang, Tingshuo, Tingwang, Tingdui, and Tingxuan. He married a woman née Li. He placed tenth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 137th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Qian Zhixuan was registered in a civilian household in Tieling Guard, Liaodong, and was a native of Changshu County in the directly administered metropolitan region. He was a guard-school student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Shunchen; he ranked first in birth order and was aged thirty-three, born on the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Tai, his grandfather was Yuanjin, his father was Biao, and his mother was née Wang. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brother Shu was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the same examination cohort; his younger brother was Zhikui. He married a woman née Xu and subsequently a woman née Chang. He placed twenty-sixth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and forty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yan Jie, registered in a civilian household in Wucheng County, Huzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a prefectural-school student specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Zijun; he ranked first in birth order and was aged twenty-nine, born on the twenty-third day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Yi (繹), who held an honorary official title for public benefactions; his grandfather was Yi (釴); his father was Yun, an annual tribute student; and his mother was née Wu. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Guo and Jian. He married a woman née Cai. He placed sixth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and thirty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Ma Fu, registered in a military household in Suizhou, Guide Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Surong; he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-eight years old, born on the eighteenth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Xian, an annual tribute student; his grandfather was Cheng; his father was Wenju; and his mother was née Zhai. His mother was still living and his father was deceased. His elder brother Qin was an Assistant Instructor; his younger brother’s name is transcribed as 𨰜 [?]. His wife was née Gao. He placed fortieth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 318th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Mao Kongchi, registered in a military household in Fuqing County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian, was an additional student of the county Confucian school specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Maodui; he ranked sixth among his brothers and was forty years old, born on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Jun; his grandfather was Wenbai; his father was Yuanwen; his mother was née Qin; and his stepmother was née Chen. His parents were deceased. His elder brother Kongyu had been granted the honorary title of Bureau Director in the Ministry of Revenue. His wife was née Chen, and his subsequent wife was née Wang. He placed twenty-ninth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 197th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Haowen, registered in a civilian household in Leting County, Luanzhou, Yongping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Yuqing; he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-four years old, born on the twenty-third day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Qin; his grandfather was Mao; his father was Chen, a Sacrificial Attendant; his mother was née Shi; and his stepmother was née Yang. His father was still living and his mother was deceased. His elder brother Haoxue was a tribute scholar (gongshi). His wife was née Li. He placed twenty-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 112th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Shi, registered in a civilian household in Yizhou, Baoding Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Zongyi; he ranked first among his brothers and was forty-one years old, born on the fifteenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Ning; his grandfather was Shiying; his father was Shou’en, a Director of Foodstuffs; his mother was née Hao; and his stepmother was née Wang. Both his parental and grandparental generations had surviving members. His younger brothers were Yang, a Sacrificial Attendant, and Zhao. His wife was née Jia, and his subsequent wife was née Hu. He placed 129th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 120th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wang Najiang, registered in Rong County, Liuzhou Prefecture, Guangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a county government student specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Yiyi; he was seventh in birth order, aged thirty-nine, and born on the eleventh day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Hui, a clerk in an office [?]; his grandfather was Hong, a Police Chief; and his father was Ru, an Assistant Prefect. His father's former wife was née Li, his principal mother was née Wu, and his birth mother was née Liu. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Nayan, a tribute scholar, and Nayi, an Instructor. He married a woman née Hu. He placed seventh in the Guangxi Provincial Examination and 306th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Han Xun, registered in the Xi'an Front Guard, Shaanxi, belonged to a military household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Zixu; he was first in birth order, aged forty, and born on the eighteenth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Duo, a Department Magistrate, who received successive posthumous honors as Grand Master for Excellent Counsel and Prefect of Daming Prefecture. His grandfather was Fu, formerly Left Vice Minister of Revenue and concurrently Left Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate. His father was Ju, a holder of a seventh-rank prestige title, and his mother was née Yao. His mother was living and his father deceased. His younger brothers were Xu and Xun. He married a woman née Wang and subsequently a woman née Li. He placed fiftieth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 219th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Deng Dong, registered in Linhai County, Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to an official household and was originally from Hanchuan County, Huguang. He was a county government student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Shaolong; he was ninth in birth order, aged thirty-nine, and born on the twenty-second day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Xuanjing, his grandfather was Hong, and his father was Xian, who had been granted the privilege of wearing official cap and belt under provisions for imperial favor. His mother was née Chen. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Song and Mi, and his younger brothers were Qi and Xiao. He married a woman née Yang. He placed tenth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 272nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lin Dachun, registered in Chaoyang County, Chaozhou Prefecture, Guangdong, belonged to a military household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Bangyang; he was first in birth order, aged twenty-eight, and born on the third day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Jing, his grandfather was Xian, his father was Shan, and his mother was née Chen. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Bangrui and Dazhi. He married a woman née Chen. He placed sixty-first in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 202nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Qian Youwei, courtesy name Weizhong, was registered in a civilian household in Changshu County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was a native of Wu County; a county government student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was second in birth order, aged twenty-six, and born on the sixth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shou, a Professor in a princely establishment; his grandfather was Pao, his father Tizhi, and his mother née Chen; his parents and at least one grandparent were living, his wife was née Su, and he ranked forty-first in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 296th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Yigui, courtesy name Shiqi, was registered in a military household in Changtai County, Zhangzhou Prefecture, Fujian; a county government student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-nine, and born on the first day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Cheng, his grandfather Zijian, his father Dunjun, and his mother née Xue; both parents were deceased, his younger brother was Yibai, his wife was née Cai, and he ranked seventieth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 226th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Sizhi, courtesy name Ziwei, was registered in a civilian household in Xinyang Subprefecture, Runing Prefecture, Henan; a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-four, and born on the seventeenth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xuan, his grandfather Jing, his father Wenying, and his mother née Yang; his mother was living and his father deceased, his wife was née Li, and he ranked twelfth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 234th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Ce, courtesy name Xiaoyu, was registered in a civilian household in Qinshui County, Zezhou Subprefecture, Shanxi; a county government student specializing in the Book of Documents, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-five, and born on the tenth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lian, his grandfather Liangzheng, who held an honorary official title granted for longevity, his father Chu, his mother née Yang, and his stepmother also née Yang; both parents were living, his younger brothers were Mo, Shi, and Zhuan, his wife was née Kang, and he ranked fifty-sixth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and ninety-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Mao Wenbang, registered in Songyang County, Chuzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Xizhou. Second in birth order, he was aged forty-one and was born on the fifteenth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Hongling; his grandfather was Jinxi, who held an honorary official title for longevity; his father was Tai; and his mother was née Liu. His mother alone was still living. His elder brother was Wenyu, and his younger brothers were Wenchong, Wenjiao, and Wenyuan. He married a woman née Xia and subsequently a woman née Qi. He ranked forty-fifth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and sixty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lin Yanggao, registered in Qiongshan County, Qiongzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Ruzhen. First in birth order, he was aged forty-one and was born on the eighth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Sheng; his grandfather was Ding; his father was Xuan; and his mother was née Wang. His mother alone was still living. His younger brothers were Yangjian, Yangyong, Yangzheng, Yangcui, and Yangchun. He married a woman née Wu. He ranked seventieth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 270th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Dechun, registered in Qingyuan County, Baoding Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Dongqing. Second in birth order, he was aged twenty-eight and was born on the fifteenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Bin; his grandfather was Jin; his father was Yong; and his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were still living. His elder brother was Shuchun. He married a woman née Peng. He ranked seventy-first in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 280th in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
臣唐汝楫
臣對臣聞帝王之致治也有敬畏之誠而後
可以弘天下之大化有當務之智而後可以
執天下之大機何謂敬畏之誠上體天心下
恤民隱精純而懇至者是也何謂當務之智
辨人才之實得任馭之宜翕受而敷施者是
也惟誠也故興道致治之具皆根于交修儆
戒之真而其治也為有本惟智也故承流宣
化之澤自得乎執簡御煩之方而其運也為
不勞治有本則王道敷于天德而天下之大
===
化以弘運不勞則端拱委于責成而天下之
大機以執是故古之帝王竭一己之誠而敬
天勤民以克盡其代天理物之責極一己之
明而選賢任能以聿臻其咸熙庶績之功愛
民以奉天知人以安民權度精切而恩惠廣
大機之所以妙運而不測也庶明勵翼而帝
力不知化之所以溥博而無疆也由是垂衣
裳而萬國寧戢兵革而四夷服泰和薰蒸災
眚不作致治之盛孰有加于此者哉欽惟
皇帝陛下亶

大機以執是故古之帝王竭一已之誠而敬
天勤民以克盡其代天理物之責極一已之
明而選賢任能以聿臻其咸熙底績之功愛
民以奉天知人以安民權度精切而恩惠廣

裳而萬國寧戢兵革而四夷服泰和薰蒸災
眚不作致治之盛孰有加于此者哉欽惟
===
皇帝陛下亶
punctuated:
臣唐汝楫。

臣對：臣聞帝王之致治也，有敬畏之誠，而後可以弘天下之大化；有當務之智，而後可以執天下之大機。何謂敬畏之誠？上體天心，下恤民隱，精純而懇至者是也。何謂當務之智？辨人才之實，得任馭之宜，翕受而敷施者是也。惟誠也，故興道致治之具，皆根于交修儆戒之真，而其治也為有本；惟智也，故承流宣化之澤，自得乎執簡御煩之方，而其運也為不勞。治有本，則王道敷于天德，而天下之大化以弘；運不勞，則端拱委于責成，而天下之大機以執。是故古之帝王，竭一己之誠，而敬天勤民，以克盡其代天理物之責；極一己之明，而選賢任能，以聿臻其咸熙庶績之功。愛民以奉天，知人以安民，權度精切而恩惠廣，大機之所以妙運而不測也；庶明勵翼而帝力不知，化之所以溥博而無疆也。由是垂衣裳而萬國寧，戢兵革而四夷服，泰和薰蒸，災眚不作，致治之盛，孰有加于此者哉？欽惟皇帝陛下亶
translation_en:
Your servant Tang Ruji.

Your servant replies: I have heard that, in bringing about good government, emperors and kings must possess the sincerity of reverence and awe before they can extend the great transforming influence throughout the realm; they must possess the wisdom to attend to urgent affairs before they can grasp the great levers of government. What is the sincerity of reverence and awe? It consists in embodying Heaven’s intent above and compassionately attending to the people’s hidden sufferings below, with purity and utmost earnestness. What is the wisdom to attend to urgent affairs? It consists in discerning people’s true abilities, finding the proper means of employing and directing them, and receiving counsel broadly and putting it into practice. Through sincerity, all the means of promoting the Way and achieving good government are rooted in genuine mutual cultivation and admonition, so that government has a foundation. Through wisdom, the benefits of carrying forward imperial influence and spreading moral transformation naturally find their proper method in grasping the essentials to manage complexities, so that the work of government proceeds without toil. When government has a foundation, the Kingly Way unfolds from heavenly virtue, and the great transforming influence throughout the realm is extended. When government proceeds without toil, the ruler sits upright with hands folded, entrusting tasks to others and holding them responsible for their accomplishment, and thus grasps the great levers of government.

Therefore, the emperors and kings of antiquity exhausted their sincerity in revering Heaven and laboring for the people, thereby fully discharging their responsibility to order all things on Heaven’s behalf. They exercised their discernment to the utmost in selecting the worthy and employing the capable, thereby attaining the achievement of making every undertaking prosper. They cherished the people in order to serve Heaven, and understood men in order to bring peace to the people. Their judgments and standards were precise and fitting, while their beneficence was far-reaching: thus the great levers of government operated wondrously and beyond comprehension. The many enlightened ministers diligently assisted them, while the emperor’s contribution went unrecognized: thus their transforming influence became all-embracing and boundless. Consequently, they let their robes hang down, and the myriad states were at peace; they put away weapons and armor, and the peoples of the four quarters submitted. Supreme harmony permeated everything, and disasters and calamities did not arise. Who could surpass such flourishing good government? Reverently considering Your Majesty the Emperor, truly …

神聖之資邃
敬一之學
中和建極
仁孝作孚

translation_en:
…endowed with divine sagacity and profound in the learning of reverent unity. Through equilibrium and harmony, Your Majesty establishes the supreme standard; through benevolence and filial piety, you inspire trust. Your consummate virtue is concentrated in profound serenity, and numinous gifts manifest auspicious signs; your wondrous achievements reach the lofty heavens, and favorable portents join in celebration. Thus today the fragrance of perfect government rises and reaches above and below; your transforming influence flows everywhere, extending throughout the Chinese realm and the foreign peoples. Such things have surely never been seen in all antiquity. Yet you remain unsatisfied with your attainments, summoning us, your servants, to court and questioning us on the way to revere Heaven and labor diligently for the people, and on strategies for showing them kindness and relief and securing their peace. From this, your servant can glimpse Your Majesty’s noble resolve: you seek the Way as though you had yet to behold it, and thirst for good government. Though I am foolish, and my learning falls shamefully short in examining antiquity, my determination to express my loyalty is earnest. Your servant considers that, in bringing about good government, the sage kings of antiquity invariably made revering Heaven and laboring diligently for the people their foremost duties. For the sovereign is Heaven’s son. The Son of Heaven takes Heaven as his father and Earth as his mother, and regards nourishing the people as his responsibility. title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:

者無不至矣故當時治化之隆冠絶古今而

…dare to indulge in play or pleasure. Revere Heaven’s changing dispositions; do not dare to rush recklessly about.” How profound was this reverence! The Book of Documents says: “He cherished and protected the common people and bestowed kindness upon widowers and widows. From morning until the sun declined past midday, he had no leisure even to eat.” How great was this diligence! Thus Yao’s vigilance, Shun’s caution, Yu’s tireless application, Tang’s trembling awe, King Wen’s protecting and watching over the people, and King Wu’s mastery through reverence and righteousness all manifested an awed respect that shone clearly within and without, and a solemn reverence uninterrupted in things manifest or hidden. When these qualities were extended into diligent government for the people, every effort was made to comfort and encourage them, correct and guide them, facilitate their use of resources and enrich their livelihoods, gather blessings and establish the supreme standard, and secure their well-being, prosperity, and sustenance. Hence the flourishing government and moral transformation of those times surpassed all ages, standing so high that nothing could excel them.
I reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao founded the realm, and Emperor Chengzu Wen inherited the great imperial undertaking. Their magnificent achievements and grand designs cannot possibly be recounted in full. Yet the greatest principles by which they established the supreme standard and handed down models consisted simply in revering Heaven and diligently caring for the people. Such writings as the record of perfect sincerity and the text on the Great Sacrifice served to exalt the sacrificial institutions and revere Heaven. Remitting taxes because of drought and distributing grain when famine was reported served to relieve hidden suffering and diligently care for the people. Their plans to bequeath peace and ease for countless generations, thereby guiding and protecting their descendants—ah, how magnificent they were! The succession of sage emperors handed down and received this single Way. Now Your Majesty has wondrously grasped its true transmission and reverently carries on…

title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
先緒益有以對揚而光大之
郊壇分祀辨正陰陽之位
欽天有記煥發昭事之忱其敬
天也可謂至矣
躬祈禱以重農事蠲雜租以濟民艱發內帑以
蘇困窮減貢獻以節冗費其勤民也可謂悉
矣
臨御以来二十九年于茲敬慎夙夜不遑寧處
盖始終如一日也方今文恬武熈內寧外謐
天下樂育于雍熈泰和之域而涵濡乎汪濊
===
浸潤之澤者亦既久矣然民歌有年之頌而
水旱饑饉或時見焉人樂承平之休而煙塵
烽鏑或竊發焉近者沴潦頻仍閭閻愁苦胡
騎猖獗邊陲驛騷夫天人之應不誣而安攘
之功有自今若此者豈惟
陛下慮之臣亦且疑之矣臣請根據其說而條陳
之夫王者求端于天而察法于地天確然示
人易也必五行四時宣其能而後彰保合太
和之化地隤然示人簡也必山岳河海運其
功而後著含弘光大之德然則人君之治天

punctuated:
先緒，益有以對揚而光大之。郊壇分祀，辨正陰陽之位；欽天有記，煥發昭事之忱。其敬天也，可謂至矣。躬祈禱以重農事，蠲雜租以濟民艱，發內帑以蘇困窮，減貢獻以節冗費。其勤民也，可謂悉矣。臨御以来二十九年于茲，敬慎夙夜，不遑寧處，盖始終如一日也。方今文恬武熈，內寧外謐，天下樂育于雍熈泰和之域，而涵濡乎汪濊浸潤之澤者，亦既久矣。然民歌有年之頌，而水旱饑饉或時見焉；人樂承平之休，而煙塵烽鏑或竊發焉。近者沴潦頻仍，閭閻愁苦，胡騎猖獗，邊陲驛騷。夫天人之應不誣，而安攘之功有自。今若此者，豈惟陛下慮之？臣亦且疑之矣。
臣請根據其說而條陳之。夫王者求端于天，而察法于地。天確然示人易也，必五行四時宣其能，而後彰保合太和之化；地隤然示人簡也，必山岳河海運其功，而後著含弘光大之德。然則人君之治天
translation_en:
…the legacy of your predecessors, further honoring it and extending its glory. By conducting separate sacrifices at the suburban altars, Your Majesty has correctly distinguished the positions of yin and yang; through a record of revering Heaven, you have splendidly expressed your heartfelt devotion to serving it illustriously. Your reverence for Heaven may indeed be called consummate. You have personally offered prayers to show the importance you attach to agriculture, remitted miscellaneous taxes to relieve the people’s hardships, disbursed funds from the palace treasury to revive those in distress and poverty, and reduced tribute offerings to curb unnecessary expenditure. Your diligent care for the people may indeed be called comprehensive. In the twenty-nine years since you ascended the throne, you have been reverent and circumspect morning and night, never allowing yourself repose: from beginning to end, you have remained as constant as on a single day.
At present, civil and military affairs are tranquil, and peace prevails both within and beyond the realm. All under Heaven have long enjoyed being nurtured in a realm of concord, prosperity, and supreme harmony, steeped in your abundant, all-pervading beneficence. Yet although the people sing praises of plentiful harvests, floods, droughts, and famine still sometimes appear; although they delight in the blessings of lasting peace, the dust of battle, beacon fires, and arrows sometimes unexpectedly arise. Recently, disastrous flooding has recurred, ordinary households have suffered grief and hardship, barbarian cavalry have run rampant, and the frontiers have been thrown into turmoil. The correspondence between Heaven and humanity is no falsehood, and success in securing peace within and repelling threats from without has its causes. With conditions now as they are, is Your Majesty alone troubled? Your servant, too, is perplexed.
Your servant begs leave to set forth these matters point by point, grounding them in their underlying principles. A king seeks his guiding principles in Heaven and examines his models in Earth. Heaven, firm and steadfast, shows humanity ease; yet only after the Five Phases and four seasons have exercised their capacities does it manifest the transforming power that preserves and unites supreme harmony. Earth, yielding and compliant, shows humanity simplicity; yet only after mountains, rivers, and seas have performed their functions does it display its virtue of embracing all, encompassing all, illuminating all, and magnifying all. Thus, in the ruler’s governance of all under Heaven…

濟之義大公之制矣臣聞天生萬物不能以

師惟其克相上帝寵綏四方聖人以一身裁
天下之務不能以獨理而命之庶職曰惟王
建國辨方正位體國經野設官分職以為民
極稽古稱盛治者莫過于唐虞三代然欽明
濬哲之德必牧岳煕載寅亮天工而後協和
時雍之治成焉寛仁勤儉之德必百僚師師
俊彥旁求而後文命覃敷兆民允殖之治成

牧分治以布之于外而後咸和永清之治成

下亦至易至簡也，而其致理圖化，當必有共濟之義、大公之制矣。臣聞天生萬物，不能以自理，而命之聖人，曰：「天佑下民，作之君，作之師，惟其克相上帝，寵綏四方。」聖人以一身裁天下之務，不能以獨理，而命之庶職，曰：「惟王建國，辨方正位，體國經野，設官分職，以為民極。」稽古稱盛治者，莫過于唐虞三代。然欽明濬哲之德，必牧岳煕載，寅亮天工，而後協和時雍之治成焉；寛仁勤儉之德，必百僚師師，俊彥旁求，而後文命覃敷、兆民允殖之治成焉。至于文武，亦必六卿率屬，以總之于內，九牧分治，以布之于外，而後咸和永清之治成焉。百姓用康，在庶官之惟敘；黎民敏德，由臣鄰之克艱，大抵然也。

translation_en:
…governing All under Heaven is likewise supremely easy and simple. Yet bringing about good order and pursuing transformation must surely require the principle of working together toward a common end and institutions founded on complete impartiality. Your servant has heard that Heaven produces the myriad things but cannot itself govern them, and therefore entrusts them to sages. As it is said: “Heaven aids the people below, providing them with rulers and teachers, that they may assist the Lord on High and cherish and pacify the four quarters.” The sage, with his single person, adjudicates the affairs of All under Heaven but cannot govern them alone, and therefore entrusts them to the various offices. As it is said: “The king establishes the state, distinguishes the directions and fixes the positions, lays out the capital and divides the countryside, establishes offices and apportions duties, thereby setting a standard for the people.” Examining antiquity, no periods celebrated for flourishing government surpass those of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Yet even with the virtues of reverence, enlightenment, profound understanding, and wisdom, the regional governors and chiefs had to discharge their duties splendidly and reverently assist Heaven’s work before a government of concord and universal harmony could be achieved. Even with the virtues of generosity, benevolence, diligence, and frugality, the hundred officials had to learn from one another, and outstanding men had to be sought far and wide, before a government in which civil instruction spread broadly and the multitude truly flourished could be achieved. As for Kings Wen and Wu, they too required the six ministers to lead their subordinates and coordinate affairs within, and the nine regional governors to administer their respective territories and extend government abroad, before universal harmony and lasting peace could be achieved. The people’s well-being depends on the orderly arrangement of the various offices; the common people’s diligence in virtue derives from the ability of the ruler’s ministers and close attendants to undertake difficult duties. This is generally how it is.
Moreover, the ruler occupies his central position with only a single person: his ears and eyes provide but one person’s hearing and sight, and his hands and feet but one person’s capacity for action. With so vast a populace and so many affairs converging upon him, not only is it impossible in practice to manage everything single-handedly, but his own person is already exhausted. Your servant has never seen anyone who, himself immersed in such toil, could bring others to ease. Thus, in these circumstances, the ruler need only grasp the great controlling mechanism of All under Heaven and plan accordingly. It is like using a rudder to steer a boat or the nock to release an arrow: the effect is wondrously swift, and nothing is difficult to accomplish. Certainly he does not illuminate each individual thing in turn, yet the flow of his virtue and beneficence reaches everywhere without limit; nor …

非事事而察之也，而神明之用兼舉而不匱矣。盖所謂廓然太公，儼然至正，泰然行其所無事，而坐收百官衆職之成功者，此爾。臣伏讀聖制曰：「水旱饑荒，苗狄不靖，民生未遂，治化未孚，豈朕誠之必有未盡者？」臣愚以為，懐山襄陵之水，不失為治世；焦山烈石之旱，不累于明王。化足以成風動，而不免于有苗之征；德足以臻時乂，而不免于鬼方之伐。是水旱夷狄之患，何代無之？殊不足為有道累也。故昔之言者曰：「天心仁愛人君，時出災異以警動之。」又曰：「帝王不患有夷狄之侵，而患無禦之之具；不貴有禦之之具，而貴吾無以致夷之窺而已。」然則今日仰答仁愛之天心，曲盡備禦之至計，是誠不可以不之講也。

translation_en:
…Nor does he scrutinize every affair individually, yet his spiritual insight operates comprehensively and is never exhausted. This is what is meant by being expansively impartial, solemnly upright, and serenely proceeding without meddling, thereby reaping, without exertion, the accomplishments of the hundred officials in their various offices. I have reverently read Your Majesty’s sacred decree: “Floods, droughts, famine, and scarcity prevail; the Miao and Di are not pacified; the people’s livelihood remains unfulfilled; and the transforming influence of government has not won their trust. Could it be that my sincerity has not yet been fully realized?” In my humble view, floods that encircled mountains and rose over hills did not prevent an age from being well governed; droughts that scorched mountains and split rocks did not discredit enlightened kings. Transforming influence sufficient to move the people as wind moves grass did not dispense with the campaign against the Youmiao; virtue sufficient to bring the age to good order did not dispense with the expedition against Guifang. In what age, then, have there been no troubles from floods, droughts, and foreign peoples? These certainly need not discredit a ruler who possesses the Way. Thus a speaker of old said: “Heaven’s heart cherishes the ruler with benevolence, and from time to time sends calamities and anomalies to warn and stir him.” Another said: “Emperors and kings worry not that foreign peoples may invade, but that they lack the means to resist them. What they prize is not possessing the means of resistance, but having nothing in their own conduct that invites foreign peoples to covet their realm.” Thus, today, to respond reverently to Heaven’s benevolent heart and to work out in every detail the best plans for preparedness and defense—these are indeed matters that must be considered.

I have also reverently read Your Majesty’s sacred decree: “Do the ministers entrusted with affairs and the officials who deal directly with the people truly embody my diligent concern for their welfare? Might they instead be idle and negligent, greedy and cruel, giving no thought to the people?” How great …

title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
皇言所謂明見萬里之外獨觀萬化之原者也臣
請發
淵衷而極論之夫變不虚生致寇有自天變之來
人心之怨也人心之怨吏治之非也今
陛下憫念黎元心固切矣而所以奉行于下者或
不能精白以承休則膏澤屯而不究矣外夷
之侵内備之弛也内備之弛將領之非也今
陛下惠養軍士政固善矣而所以分閫于外者類
多苟且以塞責則威嚴弛而不振矣嘗聞四
海之利病係于斯民之休戚斯民之休戚係
===
于守令之賢否乃今催科賦歛以效職而無
旬宣惠和之政簿書期會以程能而鮮亮采
靖共之忠甚者假上剥民為國歛怨恣意貪
饕肆行漁獵者尤可畏也夫守令之官最為
近民使天下皆若人焉則小民其有不困者
幾希雖日厪
陛下焦勞之思而斯民流離輾轉阽于危亡
陛下得而見之乎兵不能禦敵由于將非其人將
不能將兵由于用非其道乃今世胄紈袴之
豢習難以責其折衝禦侮之勇召募𧇊強之

punctuated: 皇言，所謂明見萬里之外、獨觀萬化之原者也。臣請發淵衷而極論之。夫變不虚生，致寇有自。天變之來，人心之怨也；人心之怨，吏治之非也。今陛下憫念黎元，心固切矣，而所以奉行于下者，或不能精白以承休，則膏澤屯而不究矣。外夷之侵，内備之弛也；内備之弛，將領之非也。今陛下惠養軍士，政固善矣，而所以分閫于外者，類多苟且以塞責，則威嚴弛而不振矣。嘗聞四海之利病，係于斯民之休戚；斯民之休戚，係于守令之賢否。乃今催科賦歛以效職，而無旬宣惠和之政；簿書期會以程能，而鮮亮采靖共之忠。甚者假上剥民，為國歛怨，恣意貪饕，肆行漁獵者，尤可畏也。夫守令之官，最為近民，使天下皆若人焉，則小民其有不困者幾希。雖日厪陛下焦勞之思，而斯民流離輾轉，阽于危亡，陛下得而見之乎？兵不能禦敵，由于將非其人；將不能將兵，由于用非其道。乃今世胄紈袴之豢習，難以責其折衝禦侮之勇；召募𧇊強之
translation_en:
…Your Majesty’s words exemplify what is meant by seeing clearly beyond ten thousand li and discerning, alone, the source of all transformations. Your servant asks leave to unfold Your Majesty’s profound intentions and discuss them fully. Portents do not arise without cause, and the coming of invaders has its origins. Heavenly portents arise from the people’s resentment; the people’s resentment arises from failures in local administration. Your Majesty’s concern for the common people is indeed earnest, yet those who carry out your policies below sometimes fail to receive your beneficence with pure and sincere hearts. Thus your bounty is obstructed and does not reach everywhere. Invasions by foreign peoples arise from lax domestic defenses; lax domestic defenses arise from failures among the commanders. Your Majesty’s policies for generously supporting the soldiers are indeed good, yet those entrusted with regional military commands mostly make do with expedients merely to discharge their responsibilities. Thus military authority grows slack and cannot be restored.

I have heard that the welfare and troubles of all within the four seas depend upon the people’s well-being and suffering, and that the people’s well-being and suffering depend upon whether prefects and magistrates are worthy. Yet nowadays they demonstrate their performance by pressing for tax payments and collecting levies, without policies that spread benevolence and harmony. They measure ability by registers, documents, deadlines, and accounting, while few show the loyalty of faithfully performing their duties with diligence and reverence. Worse still, those who invoke their superiors’ authority to exploit the people, accumulate resentment against the state, indulge their greed, and freely prey upon others are especially to be feared. Prefects and magistrates are the officials closest to the people. If all throughout the realm were such men, very few common people would escape hardship. Though this daily burdens Your Majesty with anxious thoughts, can Your Majesty actually see these people wandering displaced, driven from place to place, and nearing ruin and death?

Troops cannot resist the enemy because their commanders are unsuitable; commanders cannot lead troops because the methods by which they are employed are wrong. Nowadays, the pampered habits of hereditary scions and privileged sons make it difficult to demand of them the courage to repulse an enemy and resist aggression; as for the fierce and strong men [?] recruited into service …

title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
粗才初不聞乎堅瑕張弛之方甚者擅奪首
功扣除常給殘虐多端朘剥無厭者尤可畏
也夫三軍之命懸于一人使將領皆若人焉
則邊兵其有不困者幾希雖日切
陛下宵旰之憂而軍士扼腕疾視莫之控訴
陛下得而見之乎然則足國安民之道弭災禦寇
之方豈必他求哉蓋聞百官修輔則夏后之
山川以寧方叔壯猷則宣王之武功以競今
日民生之未遂守令之責耳邊圉之多警將
領之責耳
===
陛下知致弊之由曷思所以救之乎病化理之鬱
曷思所以更之乎史有之曰今之郡守民之
師帥也師帥不賢則主德不宣恩澤不流蓋
言守令之任不可不重也任守令之道大約
有三精其選嚴其課久其任而已矣必先安
靜悃愊之求鑒賢愚淆混之失重殿最核實
之條畧累資積考之說所謂秩當遷也不移
其地禄當厚也不移其官可也所謂以親民
長吏轉為郡守有績則進爵加秩者可也他
若馭之以八統察之以六條叙之以三式法

translation_en:
…men of crude ability, who have never learned the methods of handling strong and weak points or of tightening and relaxing control. Worse still, those who arbitrarily appropriate credit for heads taken in battle, withhold regular allowances, practice cruelties of every kind, and exploit their men insatiably are especially to be feared. The lives of the entire army hang upon one man. If all commanders were men of this sort, few frontier soldiers could escape distress. Though Your Majesty is daily consumed by anxiety, attending to affairs from before dawn until late at night, the soldiers wring their hands and glare in anger, with nowhere to lodge their complaints. Can Your Majesty see their plight? Must we therefore seek elsewhere for the means to enrich the state and bring peace to the people, or for methods to avert calamities and repel invaders? I have heard that when the hundred officials diligently rendered assistance, the mountains and rivers under the ruler of Xia became tranquil; and that through Fang Shu’s mighty counsels, King Xuan’s military achievements flourished. That the people’s livelihood remains unfulfilled today is the responsibility of prefects and magistrates; that the frontiers face frequent alarms is the responsibility of commanders.
Your Majesty knows the causes of these abuses: why not consider how to remedy them? You are troubled by the obstruction of moral transformation and good government: why not consider how to reform it? The histories say: “Today’s commandery governors are the people’s teachers and leaders. If their teachers and leaders are unworthy, the ruler’s virtue is not made manifest, and his beneficence does not reach them.” This means that the responsibilities of prefects and magistrates must be treated with great seriousness. There are, broadly speaking, just three principles for employing prefects and magistrates: select them carefully, assess them rigorously, and keep them long in office. One must first seek men who are calm, sincere, and devoted; take warning from the error of mixing the worthy with the foolish; give weight to provisions for verifying performance when ranking officials from worst to best; and give less weight to arguments based on accumulated seniority and successive evaluations. The saying that, when an official’s rank merits advancement, he should not be moved from his locality, and when his stipend merits an increase, he should not be moved from his office, offers an acceptable course. So too does the saying that senior officials directly responsible for the people should be promoted to commandery governors, and, if they achieve results, be advanced in noble title and official rank. title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
固亦有可行者焉志有之曰將者國之輔也
輔周則國強輔隙則國弱盖言將領之任不
可不重也任將領之道大約有三慎其簡重
其責假其權而已矣必公取舍而不以愛憎
加較勇畧而不以黷貨進功必錄而不以賤
遺罪必誅而不以親貸無持細苛而長養其
投石超距之氣可也俯從寬假而開放其摯
擊虎摶之心可也他若先之以六術繼之以
五權察之以八徵法固亦有可用者焉甄别
黜陟之典明則賢者勸而不賢者亦有所畏
===
而不敢鼓舞振作之用神則能者勉而不能
者亦知自奮以効用由是稱彊項者有砥礪
名節之董宣持風裁者有不畏貴戚之郅都
後催科者有勞心撫字之陽城敦本實者有
修明禮教之衛颯而守令得人矣守令得人
則民遂安全飽煖之欲而無咨嗟愁怨之聲
陰陽不至于繆盭氛氣不至于充塞人心訢
合而天休滋至何有乎水旱饑荒之患哉設
或數有適然災沴時作而吏稱民安本業以
固所謂有道之國天不能災地不能阨年榖

punctuated:
固亦有可行者焉。志有之曰：「將者，國之輔也；輔周則國強，輔隙則國弱。」盖言將領之任不可不重也。任將領之道，大約有三：慎其簡，重其責，假其權而已矣。必公取舍而不以愛憎加，較勇畧而不以黷貨進，功必錄而不以賤遺，罪必誅而不以親貸。無持細苛而長養其投石超距之氣，可也；俯從寬假而開放其摯擊虎摶之心，可也。他若先之以六術，繼之以五權，察之以八徵，法固亦有可用者焉。

甄别黜陟之典明，則賢者勸，而不賢者亦有所畏而不敢；鼓舞振作之用神，則能者勉，而不能者亦知自奮以効用。由是稱彊項者，有砥礪名節之董宣；持風裁者，有不畏貴戚之郅都；後催科者，有勞心撫字之陽城；敦本實者，有修明禮教之衛颯，而守令得人矣。守令得人，則民遂安全飽煖之欲，而無咨嗟愁怨之聲；陰陽不至于繆盭，氛氣不至于充塞；人心訢合，而天休滋至，何有乎水旱饑荒之患哉？設或數有適然，災沴時作，而吏稱民安，本業以固，所謂有道之國，天不能災，地不能阨，年榖
translation_en:
…there are certainly also practicable measures among these methods. A treatise says: “The general is the support of the state. When that support is complete, the state is strong; when it has gaps, the state is weak.” This means that the responsibility entrusted to military commanders must be treated with the utmost seriousness. The way to appoint commanders comprises roughly three things: exercise care in their selection, give weight to their responsibilities, and grant them authority. Selection and rejection must be impartial, without the intrusion of affection or hatred; courage and strategic ability must be assessed, without promoting men for corrupt payments. Merit must always be recorded, without overlooking men of low status; crimes must always be punished, without pardoning those who are close to oneself. It is fitting to refrain from imposing petty and exacting restrictions, thereby nurturing their spirit for such martial feats as throwing stones and leaping distances. It is fitting to accommodate them with latitude, thereby giving free rein to their spirit of striking like a bird of prey and grappling like a tiger. Other methods, such as beginning with the six arts, following these with the five expedients, and examining men through the eight signs, certainly also offer usable measures.

When the rules for distinguishing men and dismissing or promoting them are clear, the worthy are encouraged, while the unworthy likewise have something to fear and dare not act amiss. When the means of inspiring and rousing men work with marvelous efficacy, the capable exert themselves, while even the incapable know to stir themselves to useful service. Thus, among those acclaimed for their stiff-necked resolve, there will be men like Dong Xuan, who cultivated reputation and integrity; among those who uphold stern standards, men like Zhi Du, who did not fear imperial relatives and grandees; among those who give tax collection lower priority, men like Yang Cheng, who devoted their energies to caring for the people; and among those who attend earnestly to fundamentals and practical substance, men like Wei Sa, who cultivated and clarified ritual instruction. Prefectures and counties will thus have the right men in office. With the right men serving as prefects and magistrates, the people will obtain the security, sufficient food, and warmth they desire, and there will be no sounds of sighing, sorrow, or resentment. Yin and yang will not fall into disorder, nor will baleful vapors fill the world. The people’s hearts will unite in joy, and Heaven’s blessings will arrive in increasing abundance. What cause will there be to fear floods, droughts, or famine? Even if fate should happen to bring disasters from time to time, the officials will be equal to their duties, the people at peace, and their fundamental occupations secure. As the saying goes, in a state that possesses the Way, Heaven cannot bring calamity upon it, nor can Earth place it in distress; the year’s grain harvest…

title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
不登而民無菜色者固自若矣由是司督撫
者抱良平之器膺統馭者負韓白之才分閫
授鉞者必李牧魏尚其人焉據險阻要者必
張仁愿王承嗣其人焉而將領得人矣將領
得人則有摧堅制勝之具而無奔北敗衂之
虞先聲以奪其志持勝以寢其謀聞望精神
可以潛消驕悍何有乎憑陵侵軼之患哉設
或桀驁未馴梟雄反覆而養銳畜力備禦有
素所謂来則懲而禦之去則備而守之寧我
致人可常坐而役敵矣故曰聖人在上日月
===
不薄食雷發不震雨雹不為災又曰中國有
聖人海不揚波重三譯而来朝臣愚何幸而
得躬逢其盛邪雖然臣舉其要猶有可言者
焉蓋養士莫大乎學校而今之守令學校之
所儲也必謹庠序之教崇師儒之職一道德
以明禮義而不以割裂裝綴為能尊經術以
正習尚而不以規繩課試為藝如陽城之在
國子胡瑗之在鄉學則菁莪樂育之教興兔
罝好仇之才出矣故居則為端人正士出則
為循吏良臣而何慮乎守令之不賢選將莫

素所謂来則懲而禦之去則備而守之寧我
致人可常坐而役敵矣故曰聖人在上日月
===
不薄食雷發不震雨雹不為災又曰中國有
聖人海不揚波重三譯而来朝臣愚何幸而
得躬逢其盛邪雖然臣舉其要猶有可言者
焉盖養士莫大乎學校而今之守令學校之
所儲也必謹庠序之教崇師儒之職一道德
以明禮義而不以割裂裝綴為能尊經術以
正習尚而不以規繩課試為藝如陽城之在
國子胡瑗之在鄉學則菁莪樂育之教興兎
罝好仇之才出矣故居則為端人正士出則
為循吏良臣而何慮乎守令之不賢選将莫
punctuated:
不登而民無菜色者，固自若矣。由是司督撫者抱良平之器，膺統馭者負韓白之才，分閫授鉞者必李牧魏尚其人焉，據險阻要者必張仁愿王承嗣其人焉，而將領得人矣。將領得人，則有摧堅制勝之具，而無奔北敗衂之虞。先聲以奪其志，持勝以寢其謀，聞望精神可以潛消驕悍，何有乎憑陵侵軼之患哉？設或桀驁未馴，梟雄反覆，而養銳畜力，備禦有素，所謂来則懲而禦之，去則備而守之，寧我致人，可常坐而役敵矣。故曰：「聖人在上，日月不薄食，雷發不震，雨雹不為災。」又曰：「中國有聖人，海不揚波，重三譯而来朝。」臣愚何幸而得躬逢其盛邪？

雖然，臣舉其要，猶有可言者焉。蓋養士莫大乎學校，而今之守令，學校之所儲也。必謹庠序之教，崇師儒之職，一道德以明禮義，而不以割裂裝綴為能；尊經術以正習尚，而不以規繩課試為藝。如陽城之在國子，胡瑗之在鄉學，則菁莪樂育之教興，兔罝好仇之才出矣。故居則為端人正士，出則為循吏良臣，而何慮乎守令之不賢？選將莫
translation_en:
…even when the harvest fails, the people show no signs of hunger: this condition would assuredly remain unchanged. Thus, those charged with supreme command and provincial oversight would possess the capacities of Zhang Liang and Chen Ping; those entrusted with military command would have the talents of Han Xin and Bai Qi. Those granted regional commands and invested with the battle-axe of authority would surely be men like Li Mu and Wei Shang; those occupying defensible terrain and strategic positions would surely be men like Zhang Renyuan and Wang Chengsi [?]. The military commands would thereby be filled with the right men. With the right men in command, there would be the means to break strong resistance and secure victory, without fear of rout or defeat. Their reputation, preceding them, would break the enemy’s resolve; their command of victory would forestall the enemy’s schemes. Their prestige and spirit could quietly dissolve arrogance and ferocity. How, then, could there be any danger of aggression and incursions? Even if the unruly remained unsubdued and fierce chieftains proved treacherous, our men would have nurtured their fighting spirit and conserved their strength, with defensive preparations long established. As the saying goes, when they come, punish and repel them; when they withdraw, remain prepared and keep watch. Let us be the ones who compel others to come: we could constantly remain at ease while making the enemy toil. Thus it is said: “When a sage rules above, the sun and moon suffer no eclipses; thunder sounds without wreaking destruction; rain and hail cause no calamity.” It is also said: “When there is a sage in the Central Kingdom, the sea raises no waves, and people come to court through successive interpreters.” How fortunate is your foolish servant to witness such flourishing in person!

Nevertheless, in setting forth the essentials, your servant still has something to say. For nurturing scholars, nothing is more important than schools; and today’s prefects and county magistrates are men whom the schools have prepared. Instruction in the schools must be carefully attended to, and the office of learned teachers held in esteem. Moral teaching must be unified so as to clarify ritual propriety and righteousness, without treating the cutting up and piecing together of texts as an accomplishment. Classical learning must be honored so as to rectify habits and prevailing practices, without treating conformity to examination rules as mastery. If there were men like Yang Cheng at the Directorate of Education and Hu Yuan in the local schools, then the joyful nurturing celebrated in “Luxuriant Southernwood” would flourish, and worthy men fit to be “good companions,” as celebrated in “The Rabbit Net,” would emerge. In private life they would be upright and honorable scholars; on entering office they would be conscientious administrators and worthy ministers. Why, then, worry that prefects and county magistrates might be unworthy? For selecting generals, nothing…

title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
大乎武舉而今之將領武舉之所拔也必申
勅騎射之技兼舉文事之科深于兵法明經
者隸其事而庸妄不之用親試其勇而有謀
者待以不次之位而章句不之取不率教者
不得舉于鄉不有實學者不得舉于司馬則
仁義忠信之道明奇正機權之畧諳矣故無
事則為帷幄賛畫之臣有事則為干城腹心
之將而何慮乎將領之不賢雖然臣究其本
猶有可言者焉孔子曰為政在人言安民之
本于知人也取人以身言知人之本于自治
===
也知人之哲盡則安民之惠行純心之本端
斯用賢之道得此古今不易之定論也況乎
人君以一人之聞見而欲盡天下之賢才力
既不能日亦不給是故議道自已以守至正
恭已南面建其有極夫然後明目達聰廣四
方之視聽鑑空衡平定百職之妍媸孰有能
遁其情者哉于是乎人必稱官官必稱職大
小臣工罔不淬礪篤忠修明職守政治彰教
化洽而海內晏然矣董子所謂正心以正朝
廷正朝廷以正百官正百官以正萬民正此

廷正朝廷以正百官正百官以正萬民正此
punctuated:
大乎武舉，而今之將領，武舉之所拔也。必申勅騎射之技，兼舉文事之科，深于兵法明經者隸其事，而庸妄不之用；親試其勇而有謀者，待以不次之位，而章句不之取。不率教者，不得舉于鄉；不有實學者，不得舉于司馬。則仁義忠信之道明，奇正機權之畧諳矣。故無事則為帷幄賛畫之臣，有事則為干城腹心之將，而何慮乎將領之不賢？
雖然，臣究其本，猶有可言者焉。孔子曰：「為政在人。」言安民之本于知人也。「取人以身。」言知人之本于自治也。知人之哲盡，則安民之惠行；純心之本端，斯用賢之道得。此古今不易之定論也。
況乎人君以一人之聞見，而欲盡天下之賢才，力既不能，日亦不給。是故議道自已，以守至正；恭已南面，建其有極。夫然後明目達聰，廣四方之視聽；鑑空衡平，定百職之妍媸，孰有能遁其情者哉？于是乎人必稱官，官必稱職，大小臣工罔不淬礪篤忠，修明職守，政治彰，教化洽，而海內晏然矣。董子所謂「正心以正朝廷，正朝廷以正百官，正百官以正萬民」，正此
translation_en:
…nothing is more important than the military examinations, and today’s commanders are selected through them. Standards in mounted archery must be reiterated and enforced, while examinations in literary learning must also be held. Those deeply versed in military methods and conversant with the Classics should be assigned to these duties [?], while the mediocre and reckless should not be employed. Those personally tested and found both courageous and resourceful should be accorded rank outside the ordinary sequence of promotion; those versed merely in textual exposition should not be selected. Those who do not follow instruction must not be recommended at the provincial level; those without substantial learning must not be recommended to the Ministry of War. Then the principles of benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness will be understood, and the strategies of unorthodox and orthodox operations, tactical opportunity, and expedient action will be thoroughly mastered. In times of peace they will serve as ministers assisting with plans in the command tent; in times of trouble they will serve as trusted generals, shields and walls of the state. Why, then, need one fear that commanders will lack worthiness?
Nevertheless, when your servant investigates the root of the matter, there is still something to say. Confucius said, “The conduct of government depends upon men.” This means that bringing peace to the people is rooted in knowing men. “Select men by reference to one’s own person.” This means that knowing men is rooted in governing oneself. When discernment in judging men is fully developed, the benefits of bringing peace to the people can be realized. When the foundation—the purification of the mind—is correctly established, the proper way to employ the worthy is attained. This is a settled principle, unchanging from antiquity to the present.
Moreover, if a ruler wishes to encompass all the worthy and talented men of the realm through what one person alone hears and sees, his powers will be insufficient, and neither will his days suffice. Therefore, he must deliberate upon the Way himself, holding fast to perfect rectitude; he must maintain a reverent bearing as he faces south and establish the supreme standard. Only then can he make his sight keen and his hearing perceptive, extending what he sees and hears to the four quarters. With a mirror clear and scales level, he can determine the merits and defects of those holding the hundred offices. Who could then conceal his true character? Thus each man will be suited to his office, and each official will fulfill his duties. Officials great and small will all temper themselves, deepen their loyalty, and diligently discharge their responsibilities. Good government will become manifest, moral instruction will spread everywhere, and all within the seas will be at peace. Master Dong’s saying, “Rectify the mind in order to rectify the court; rectify the court in order to rectify the hundred officials; rectify the hundred officials in order to rectify the myriad people,” refers precisely to this…

title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
謂也仰惟
陛下敬一持心無逸示訓敦操存涵養之功懋時
敏日新之學所以正其心者已無不盡矣則
夫取人以身之則純心用賢之本臣復何言
哉抑臣聞之書曰慎厥終惟其始盖言銳于
始者未必繼于終而勝于暫者或不持于久
故四時常運不息其機日月貞明不改其度
上者法天以行健不輟其功純亦而不已聖
學之所以光明也夙夜而不怠基命之所以
宥密也今
===
陛下齋慄對越之心勿懈須臾惻怛慈惠之念無
少瑕翳固矣然理欲危微之辨間不容髮操
舍出入之防實則無時是故作之以憂勤矣
而或乗之以因循出之以誠篤矣而或勝之
以儀文防微杜漸之戒省察克治之功少有
弗至竊恐虛靈之體必將窒而不達裁制之
用亦有發而不當者矣臣願
陛下始終惟一而不雜于二三自強不息而無有
乎間斷防閑于莫見莫顯之際敬謹于不言
不動之時端莊靜一凝其真也明通公溥植

謂也。仰惟陛下敬一持心，無逸示訓，敦操存涵養之功，懋時敏日新之學，所以正其心者已無不盡矣。則夫取人以身之則，純心用賢之本，臣復何言哉？抑臣聞之，《書》曰：「慎厥終，惟其始。」盖言銳于始者未必繼于終，而勝于暫者或不持于久。故四時常運，不息其機；日月貞明，不改其度。上者法天以行健，不輟其功。純亦而不已，聖學之所以光明也；夙夜而不怠，基命之所以宥密也。
今陛下齋慄對越之心勿懈須臾，惻怛慈惠之念無少瑕翳，固矣。然理欲危微之辨，間不容髮；操舍出入之防，實則無時。是故作之以憂勤矣，而或乗之以因循；出之以誠篤矣，而或勝之以儀文。防微杜漸之戒，省察克治之功，少有弗至，竊恐虛靈之體必將窒而不達，裁制之用亦有發而不當者矣。臣願陛下始終惟一而不雜于二三，自強不息而無有乎間斷，防閑于莫見莫顯之際，敬謹于不言不動之時。端莊靜一，凝其真也；明通公溥，植
translation_en:
…this is precisely what is meant. I reverently consider that Your Majesty maintains your mind through reverent singleness and sets forth the admonition against ease. You diligently cultivate the work of preserving and nourishing the mind, and devote yourself to timely, assiduous learning and daily renewal. You have thus left nothing undone in rectifying your mind. What more could your servant say concerning taking your own person as the standard for selecting men, or purifying the mind as the foundation for employing the worthy? Yet your servant has heard these words from the Book of Documents: “Be as careful at the end as at the beginning.” This means that those zealous at the outset do not necessarily sustain their efforts to the end, and those who excel for a moment may not maintain this for long. Thus the four seasons revolve continually, their workings never ceasing; the sun and moon remain constant in their brightness, never altering their courses. The ruler models himself on Heaven’s vigorous activity and never interrupts his efforts. Purity likewise without cessation [?] is what makes sagely learning luminous; unremitting effort morning and night is what makes the foundations of the mandate profound and secure.
Now Your Majesty’s heart, solemn and trembling as you stand before Heaven, assuredly never slackens for an instant, and your thoughts of compassion, kindness, and generosity have not the slightest blemish or obscuration. Yet in distinguishing principle from desire, and the precarious from the subtle, there is not room for a hair’s breadth of error; vigilance over the mind’s retention and abandonment, its departures and returns, must indeed be maintained at all times. Thus, though one rouses oneself through anxious diligence, habitual laxity may take advantage of it; though one acts out of sincerity and earnestness, ceremonial form may prevail over them. If vigilance in checking the slightest beginnings of error and arresting their growth, or the work of self-examination and self-mastery, falls short in the least, your servant fears that the mind’s empty and numinous substance will become obstructed and fail to penetrate, and that its exercise of judgment and control will sometimes issue in inappropriate action. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would maintain singleness from beginning to end, unmixed with divided or wavering purposes; strengthen yourself ceaselessly, without interruption; guard yourself where things are most hidden and subtle; and remain reverent and cautious when neither speaking nor acting. Through dignity, composure, tranquility, and singleness, consolidate your inner genuineness; through clarity, comprehension, impartiality, and breadth, establish…

title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
其本也慎密緝熈聨其間也長永貞固恒其
德也根柢于一心而顯設于庶務卷之于退
蔵之密而達之于酬酢之神誠由此立智由
此出化由此弘機由此執以此事
天則恐懼不弛以此治民則曲成不遺以此任賢
則有克知灼見之明以此立政則妙裁成經
緯之用行于朝廷而羣工率職矣布于邦國
而百姓樂業矣洋溢于蠻貊而四夷来王矣
充塞于穹壤而萬物蕃育矣三光凝七政齊
諸福駢集百嘉鬯遂天德孚而王道終矣此

其本也，慎密緝熈聨其間也，長永貞固恒其德也。根柢于一心而顯設于庶務，卷之于退蔵之密而達之于酬酢之神。誠由此立，智由此出，化由此弘，機由此執。以此事天，則恐懼不弛；以此治民，則曲成不遺；以此任賢，則有克知灼見之明；以此立政，則妙裁成經緯之用。行于朝廷，而羣工率職矣；布于邦國，而百姓樂業矣；洋溢于蠻貊，而四夷来王矣；充塞于穹壤，而萬物蕃育矣。三光凝，七政齊，諸福駢集，百嘉鬯遂，天德孚而王道終矣。此端本澄源之道，聖修神化之極，實臣愚所惓惓懇望于今日者也。
陛下不棄芻蕘，留神省覧，天下幸甚，臣愚幸甚。干冒天威，不勝戰慄隕越之至。謹對。
translation_en:
…its foundation; careful vigilance and sustained illumination connect its workings; enduring steadfastness makes its virtue constant. Rooted in the single mind, it becomes manifest in the manifold affairs of government. Withdrawn, it rests in the secrecy of inward concealment; brought forth, it reaches the wondrous responsiveness of dealings with others. Through this, sincerity is established, wisdom emerges, transforming influence spreads, and the pivotal springs of action are grasped. By serving Heaven in this way, reverent fear will never slacken; by governing the people in this way, each will be brought to fulfillment without omission; by employing the worthy in this way, there will be the discernment to know them truly and see them clearly; by establishing government in this way, the work of shaping and ordering affairs will attain consummate subtlety. Practiced at court, it will bring all officials to discharge their duties; extended throughout the realm, it will enable the people to pursue their livelihoods contentedly; overflowing among the Man and Mo peoples, it will bring the peoples of the four quarters to acknowledge your kingship; filling heaven and earth, it will cause all things to flourish and multiply. The three celestial lights will be steady, and the seven celestial regulators harmonious. Every blessing will gather in abundance, and all auspicious things will flourish freely. Heaven’s virtue will command trust, and the Kingly Way will reach fulfillment. This way of setting the root aright and clearing the source, this ultimate attainment of sagely cultivation and wondrous transformation, is what your foolish servant earnestly and devotedly hopes for today.
If Your Majesty does not discard these words of a grass cutter and firewood gatherer, but attends to and examines them, it will be the greatest good fortune for all under Heaven and for your foolish servant. Having presumed to trespass upon your heavenly majesty, I am overcome with trembling and dread of falling into error. Respectfully submitted in reply.

title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
臣呂調陽
臣對臣聞帝王之御天下也固必有格天化
民之心以立其本亦必有奉天子民之政以
達其用心也者原於精神念慮之微雖存諸
中而實所以立是政之本政也者見於法制
品節之詳雖顯諸外而實所以達是心之用

Your servant, Lü Diaoyang.

Your servant replies: I have heard that when emperors and kings govern all under Heaven, they must surely possess the resolve to move Heaven and transform the people, thereby establishing the foundation; they must also conduct government that serves Heaven and treats the people as their children, thereby bringing that resolve into effect. The mind originates in the subtle workings of spirit and thought. Though it resides within, it is precisely what establishes the foundation of government. Government manifests itself in the particulars of laws, institutions, distinctions, and regulations. Though it appears outwardly, it is precisely what brings the mind’s purposes into effect. Thus, when there is a resolve to move Heaven and transform the people, heavenly virtue is cultivated beforehand, and what is applied in government is more than mere laws. When there is government that serves Heaven and treats the people as their children, the Kingly Way reaches everywhere, and what is held in the mind is more than mere good intentions. The mind directs it; government puts it into practice. It was simply by following this way that the emperors and kings of antiquity fully realized reverence for Heaven and diligent care for the people.

As for later ages, rulers might possess such a resolve; yet if their minds were not wholly in accord with heavenly virtue, their innermost thoughts could not escape the fault of mingling truth with falsehood, and thus could not provide a foundation for moving Heaven and transforming the people. They might also possess such governmental measures; yet if their government were not wholly in accord with the Kingly Way, their actions could not escape a profusion of empty formalities and trivial details, and thus could not be said to fulfill the purpose of serving Heaven and treating the people as their children. Consequently, although what they established in their own times was not without merit, the harmonious and flourishing rule of profound peace was seen no more.

Once the course of adversity had reached its extreme, the way of prosperity arose. title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝陛下
敬一以宅衷
慈仁以廣愛王心純矣憲
天以立極通變以宜民王政舉矣休徵嘉應之迭
見薄海外內之寧謐王化臻矣然猶不以已
治已安為自慊而必以大順大化為未能廼
進臣等而降
賜清問惓惓以敬
天勤民之治為圖臣捧誦拜讀之餘而有以知
陛下求治之心之切矣顧臣學術疎淺智識愚昧
===
何足以仰承
休德之萬一乎雖然敕命之歌交賡於無虞之
時如傷之視加意於不冒之眾帝王望治無
窮之心也皇天眷命猶陳儆戒之謨萬邦作
乂不廢幾康之弼人臣愛君無已之念也今
陛下有望治無窮之心而臣愚乏忠愛無已之念
是上負
朝廷下負所學矣疇昔之期待者謂何而可如
此乎盖必不敢也臣請殫心畢慮為
陛下陳之臣惟人君宅中國大以撫萬邦奉乎天

陛下陳之臣惟人君宅中圖大以撫萬邦奉乎天
punctuated:
皇帝陛下，敬一以宅衷，慈仁以廣愛，王心純矣；憲天以立極，通變以宜民，王政舉矣；休徵嘉應之迭見，薄海外內之寧謐，王化臻矣。然猶不以已治已安為自慊，而必以大順大化為未能，廼進臣等而降賜清問，惓惓以敬天勤民之治為圖。臣捧誦拜讀之餘，而有以知陛下求治之心之切矣。顧臣學術疎淺，智識愚昧，何足以仰承休德之萬一乎？

雖然，敕命之歌交賡於無虞之時，如傷之視加意於不冒之眾，帝王望治無窮之心也；皇天眷命，猶陳儆戒之謨，萬邦作乂，不廢幾康之弼，人臣愛君無已之念也。今陛下有望治無窮之心，而臣愚乏忠愛無已之念，是上負朝廷，下負所學矣。疇昔之期待者謂何，而可如此乎？盖必不敢也。臣請殫心畢慮，為陛下陳之。

臣惟人君宅中國，大以撫萬邦，奉乎天
translation_en:
…Your Imperial Majesty maintains reverent single-mindedness within your heart and extends your love through compassion and benevolence: the kingly heart is pure. You model yourself on Heaven to establish the supreme standard and adapt to changing circumstances to benefit the people: kingly government is enacted. Auspicious signs and favorable responses appear repeatedly, and tranquility prevails throughout the lands within and beyond the seas: kingly transformation has reached its fulfillment. Yet you do not rest content with order and peace already achieved. Instead, you regard supreme harmony and comprehensive moral transformation as still unattained. Thus you have summoned us and graciously bestowed your searching questions, earnestly seeking government that reveres Heaven and diligently cares for the people. After respectfully receiving, reciting, and reading them, I have come to understand the intensity of Your Majesty’s desire for good government. Yet my learning is shallow and my understanding benighted: how could I possibly respond adequately to even one ten-thousandth of your splendid virtue?

Nevertheless, songs urging heed to Heaven’s mandate were sung in response to one another in times free from anxiety, and solicitous care, as though tending the injured, was extended even to people who had committed no offense [?]. Such is the inexhaustible desire of emperors and kings for good government. Even when August Heaven bestowed its favor and mandate, ministers still offered counsels of warning and admonition; even when the myriad states were well governed, they did not cease assisting through vigilance over incipient developments and concern for public well-being. Such is the unending devotion with which ministers love their sovereign. Now Your Majesty possesses an inexhaustible desire for good government. If I, foolish as I am, lacked this unending sense of loyalty and love, I would betray the court above and my own learning below. What would become of the hopes I have long cherished? How could I behave thus? Certainly I would never dare. I beg leave to devote all my heart and thought to setting these matters before Your Majesty.

I submit that the ruler dwells in the central realm, broadly cherishing the myriad states [?], and serves Heaven…

title: 嘉靖二十九年進士登科錄
text:
而為之子天心之未順子道之有虧也統乎
民而作之父母民生之未遂父母之未盡也
是其任誠匪輕其事誠匪易矣而其所以圖
為之者則有本焉心是已有用焉政是已心
足以格天化民而內聖之本立政足以奉天
子民而外王之用行人君治天下夫亦脩此
二者而已然究而言之曰天曰民其分不同
而理則相通曰敬曰勤其事不同而效則相
因故知所以敬天者未必不勤恤於民知所
以勤民者未必非善事天者也書曰惟天惠
===
民惟辟奉天又曰天佑下民作之君作之師
然則天矜于民民之所欲天必從之者也人
君誠能加意於民則所以克享天心者豈外
是哉稽古汚隆升降之迹率由於此堯之欽
天舜之勅天人知之矣而不知其平章協和
柔遠能邇者乃其敬天之實也禹之克謹天
戒湯之奉若天命人知之矣而不知其平土
粒食克寬克仁者乃其敬天之實也文之肅
將天威武之恭天成命人知之矣而不知其
發政施仁敷佑四方者乃其敬天之實也是
